Science Fiction writers, like all fiction authors, must create a story line that readers can imagine themselves being a central part of. What's the best way to find out if an article is credible?

Check their sources, check other sites to see if they come to the same conclusions. Check other articles on the website, journal or publisher to see if they do good work or let anyone publish anything.

It takes time to begin but once you know the shitty sources you can just filter those out instead of researching each article.

First, what /u/Keeok said.

Some specifics:

An article that only references articles on the same site is likely worthless.

Anyone that quotes "a study" and/or "experts" without linking to the study or naming the experts is worthless.

Some online "publications" develop reputations for pushing a point of view. This isn't necessarily bad. For instance, if you want to know why Clinton's misuse of classified information is a big deal- and it is- you won't find anything at Slate or Rolling Stone. But it is important to understand the bias the article's coming from. If you understand the bias, you can look for other points of view and have more information for your own opinions.

Anything you read online about health and nutrition that doesn't come from a reputable medical publication is worthless. Nutrition is complicated- far more so than "Mommy Blogs" and activist sites would have you believe. Rules 1 and 2 are extremely important here with this issue. Exercise isn't exactly an exception, but I've found good exercise information more common on the internet than other areas of health and nutrition.

If you react skeptically to everything you read, you'll get into the habit of looking for ways to contradict and disprove the things you read. This is a good thing. It short circuts cognative biases and forces you to gather more information.

Mine the footnotes!

Once you start doing this you will quickly see that articles are citing multiple papers, but all of those papers are citing other papers that are citing only one or two actual studies and independent ideas on a topic.

So lets look at this in reverse. Someone does a study on something, anything, and writes a paper on it. Someone else comes along and also writes on that same study. Fair enough, but then something interesting happens with the third writter, he uses the first two papers as sources for his paper when he is writing about the same study. The fourth author comes along and cites the other three as sources. By the time you have the fifth writer he uses the four additional papers for his paper concerning the same research, and suddenly he doesn't need as many additional outside sources, because four other authors have just come to the same conclusion as he did. We have a consensus! Except we really don't, see the issue here?

Then they have conventions to celebrate that they all found the same conclusion, even though they just built off of one another in an academic like circlejerk.

In addition to what other people said about checking sources I'd like to add finding the site that broke the story.

For example sometimes its a local news station or news paper that broke the story. Find their original report. Usually, it'll have more accurate facts and less sensational bullshit. The more places that republish the story the more bs gets added to it.

Develop the ability to distinguish the honest thinker from the extremist and the crank. If you can imagine that the article might be cited by a Cruz or Trump supporter, or by a Sanders supporter, it's not credible. Then, check the references, and repeat the process. If you don't find any extremists or cranks after three or four iterations of this process, you've probably found a credible article.
